title: The Victory of Asymmetry in the Iran War | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Froman argues the Iran war, 230 days in, has met many US military goals but shown the power of asymmetry: Iran's Hormuz leverage, Houthi strikes on Riyadh and attacks on US bases are reshaping Gulf security, energy prices and the regional order, possibly spurring nuclear proliferation.

themes.theme: Asymmetry as the war's main outcome

insights.claim: With relatively few missiles, drones and mines, Iran turned its control of the Strait of Hormuz into an economic weapon that projects power across the global economy despite lacking the firepower to beat the US.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Hormuz risk premia in energy and shipping may persist even if fighting pauses.
insights.quote: The most significant outcome of the war may well prove to be the power of asymmetry.

insights.claim: The Houthis, a poorly funded group, are able to upset Saudi Arabia's multi-trillion-dollar, multi-decade modernization strategy, a second example of asymmetric leverage.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Gulf-based investment themes carry tail risk from cheap weapons.
insights.locator: To think that the poorly funded but scrappy Houthis

insights.claim: Iran's willingness to threaten a possible attack on RAF Fairford, a NATO ally's base, led the US to remove long-range B-1 bombers from the UK, signalling Iranian confidence despite the damage it has taken since February.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Terror and sabotage risk to Western military and infrastructure sites is elevated.
insights.locator: The long arm of Iran is also being felt

insights.claim: The Trump administration's stated war aims were destroying Iran's air force, navy, missile launch capability and missile and drone factories, and Froman judges much of this achieved, leaving Iran with fewer military capabilities and a more strained economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Military objectives largely met, but the strategic ledger is mixed.
insights.locator: On the basis of these goals

insights.claim: The war has cost twenty-one US service members and over a thousand Iranian civilians, and depleted Patriot interceptors and THAAD batteries needed elsewhere, straining US force posture in the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Interceptor depletion points to defense-munitions demand and Indo-Pacific vulnerability.
insights.locator: Tragically, the lives of twenty-one U.S. service members

insights.claim: If Operation Epic Fury aimed to stop Iran projecting power beyond its borders, it might have had the opposite effect.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Contradicts the official success narrative; watch for Iranian escalation outside its borders.
insights.locator: More broadly, though, if the goal of Operation Epic Fury

themes.theme: Energy prices and the Russian diesel deal

insights.claim: Energy price, inflation and affordability pressure from Iran's Hormuz leverage led Trump to agree with Putin to allow the sale of millions of barrels of Russian diesel, funding Russia's war machine and opening a rift with Europe and Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Hormuz disruption transmits to US politics and sanctions policy; diesel supply stays a pressure point.
insights.locator: The resulting repercussions on energy prices

insights.claim: After Houthi strikes on Riyadh's airport killed over a dozen people, executives from Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell, BP and TotalEnergies canceled travel to Riyadh for the WPC Energy Congress.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Major oil executives treating Riyadh as unsafe is a signal for Gulf risk pricing.
insights.locator: On Monday, senior global energy executives

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, ten days away, is central to Mohammed bin Salman's plan to diversify from energy toward technology, tourism and entertainment, and Froman expects flights into Riyadh to be half-empty at best.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Weak FII attendance would hit Saudi diversification and capital-inflow sentiment.
insights.locator: The kingdom is set to host another big global event

insights.claim: Iran has inverted the logic of the thirteen US regional bases: partner countries once sought them for security but now see them as targets, and they doubt the US will defend them.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Gulf basing and security arrangements may be renegotiated, affecting defense and infrastructure plans.
insights.locator: Iran has turned the logic of those bases on its head

insights.claim: After Iranian strikes damaged bases, the US withdrew certain forces while deploying more mobile capabilities, including a third carrier strike group and an additional Marine Expeditionary Unit.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Shift toward mobile naval power rather than fixed bases.
insights.locator: After Iranian strikes damaged these bases

insights.claim: The Iran war will almost certainly accelerate the US drawdown from costly Middle East wars, likely triggering a frantic realignment of regional politics and alliance networks.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Regional power vacuum raises geopolitical volatility and new alliances.
insights.locator: The long and drawn-out process of winding down

insights.claim: Regional partners may form a Middle Eastern NATO-like lattice, with the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, or the Abraham Accords grouping, as candidate frameworks.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: New security blocs could reshape defense procurement and trade ties.
insights.locator: The recent Mecca Joint Defense Agreement

insights.claim: Without the US umbrella, Saudi Arabia and the UAE may ultimately pursue nuclear weapons, an ironic result of strikes meant to prevent proliferation.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Proliferation risk is a tail scenario for Gulf geopolitics and uranium or nuclear policy.
insights.locator: it's ironic that we may end up seeing additional countries

insights.claim: Tehran is weaker than ever yet stronger than it expected, and the regime has shown resilience, so it may remain a long-term participant in Middle East geopolitics that others must live with.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Do not price a quick regime collapse; negotiations face a regime aware of its mixed position.
insights.quote: Tehran today is weaker than it’s ever been and stronger than it almost certainly expected to be
insights.locator: What is to come for Iran

insights.claim: Reporting suggests the US might be planning an escalation of attacks, even as the Iranian regime is seen as increasingly fragile.
insights.speaker: Michael Froman
insights.so_what: Escalation risk remains alongside talk of agreement.
